headline: The Construction Foreman Foundation
threshold: By Lesson 10, you can greet your crew, give times, counts and measurements, describe conditions on site, ask basic questions, make polite requests and ask for help in Spanish, and start Construction Foreman Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Sounds and Greetings
lessons.objective: Say jobsite words clearly and greet your crew and coworkers in Spanish.
lessons.focus: The five vowels, ch, j, ll, rr and the written accent in tool names; greetings

words.note: Spanish vowels are short and pure: a as in 'father', o as in 'more'.
ch sounds like English 'church'.
j is a strong breathy h: HEH-feh. For a woman: la jefa.
ll sounds like English y in Mexico: YAH-veh. Also means key or faucet.
rr is a rolled r; ll sounds like y: ca-rre-TI-ya.
Stress falls on -ti-: mar-TI-yo.
A single r between vowels is a quick tap, like the dd in 'ladder'.
Stress on -da-: an-DA-mio.
The written accent marks the stressed syllable: ca-MIÓN.
b between vowels is soft, with lips barely touching.
Formal. With a coworker you know well: ¿Cómo estás?

words.en: How do you say "hard hat" in Spanish?

lessons.speaking: Greet a crew member, say your name, and ask how to say a tool in Spanish, then repeat the tool name clearly.

lessons.title: Numbers, Time and Measurements
lessons.objective: Give start times, counts and lengths in feet and inches for boards, bags and concrete.
lessons.focus: Numbers 0 to 1,000, clock time, and feet, inches, pounds and yards on site

words.note: Plural pies: 8 pies = 8 feet.
Concrete is ordered in yardas cúbicas (cubic yards).
Many crews just say la cinta.

words.en: We start at 7 in the morning.
words.es: Empezamos a las 7 de la mañana.

words.note: Use de for a measurement: tablas de 8 pies.

words.es: La pared mide 10 pies y 6 pulgadas.

words.en: The truck is bringing 9 yards of concrete.
words.es: El camión trae 9 yardas de concreto.

words.en: Each bag weighs 94 pounds, according to the label.
words.es: Cada saco pesa 94 libras, según la etiqueta.

lessons.speaking: Tell a crew member what time the crew starts and stops, and read them the length of 3 boards in feet and inches.

lessons.title: Ser and Estar
lessons.objective: Say who people are on site and describe what is broken, loose, level or dry.
lessons.focus: ser for what something or someone is, estar for its condition or location

words.note: For a woman: la carpintera.
Same word for a woman, with la: la electricista.
rota with feminine nouns: la escalera está rota.
Concreto fresco is concrete that has not set.

words.en: I'm the foreman on this job.
words.es: Soy el mayordomo de esta obra.
words.note: Mayordomo is common on US jobsites; capataz is also used. ser: who you are.

words.en: He's a carpenter and she's an electrician.
words.es: Él es carpintero y ella es electricista.
words.note: No un or una after ser for a job.
estar: a condition that can change.

words.en: The tools are in the truck.
words.es: Las herramientas están en la troca.
words.note: estar for location. Troca is common US Spanish for pickup truck.

lessons.speaking: Describe the site to a crew member: say who each worker is and whether the scaffold, the wall and the concrete are loose, level or dry.

lessons.title: Have, There Is, Need and Want
lessons.objective: Say what PPE and materials you have, need or want, and what everyone has to do.
lessons.focus: tener, hay, necesitar, querer and hay que + infinitive for PPE and materials

words.note: Feminine noun that takes el: el agua fría.

words.en: Do you have your hard hat?
Everyone has to wear safety glasses.
words.es: Hay que usar lentes de seguridad.
words.note: hay que + infinitive: a rule for everyone, no specific person.

words.en: I need a box of nails.
Do you want to work Saturday?

lessons.speaking: Check a new worker's PPE: ask if they have gloves, glasses and boots, and say what the crew needs today.

lessons.title: Go, Do and Can
lessons.objective: Say where you are going, what the crew is going to do, and what you can do.
lessons.focus: ir, ir a + infinitive for plans, hacer and poder for jobsite tasks

words.note: Common Mexican term; some crews say la forma.

words.en: I'm going to the hardware store.
We're going to pour the concrete tomorrow.
words.es: Vamos a colar el concreto mañana.
words.note: Colar is the common Mexican verb for pouring concrete; echar also works.

words.en: They're going to build the formwork.
words.es: Ellos van a hacer la cimbra.

words.en: I can drive the forklift; I'm certified.
words.es: Yo puedo manejar el montacargas; tengo certificación.

words.en: Juan is going to the roof.
words.note: a + el = al.

lessons.speaking: Tell a coworker where you are going now, what the crew is going to do tomorrow, and one task you can do.

lessons.title: Present Tense
lessons.objective: Say who does each task on site using regular present-tense verbs.
lessons.focus: Present-tense -ar, -er, -ir endings for yo, tú, usted, nosotros and ellos

words.note: Common in Mexico and the US; some say el sheetrock.
tú is fine between coworkers; -ar: corto, cortas, corta.

words.es: Nosotros limpiamos la obra a las 4.

words.en: They carry the blocks up to the second floor.
words.es: Ellos suben los bloques al segundo piso.
words.note: -ir verb: subo, subes, sube, subimos, suben.

words.en: I sweep and they pick up the trash.
words.es: Yo barro y ellos recogen la basura.
words.note: -er verbs: barro, barres, barre, barremos, barren.

words.en: You mix the sand with the cement.
words.es: Tú mezclas la arena con el cemento.

lessons.speaking: Split today's tasks with a coworker: say who cuts, who carries the blocks up and who cleans the site.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.objective: Ask what, who, where, when, how many and why about tasks, plans and permits on site.
lessons.focus: Question words qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo, por qué, cuál

words.note: Use ¿cuántas? with feminine nouns: ¿cuántas tablas?
Two words with an accent for 'why'; porque, one word, means 'because'.
Often plural: los planos.

words.en: How many boards are we missing?

words.note: In Mexico ¿cuál? often goes before a noun; ¿qué escalera? also works.

lessons.speaking: Ask a crew member where the blueprints are, who has the permit, and when the inspector is coming.

lessons.title: No, Never and How Much
lessons.objective: Say what is missing, what has not arrived yet, and when you need more, less or another.
lessons.focus: no, nunca, nadie, nada, todavía no, más, menos and otro on the jobsite

words.note: Use otra with feminine nouns, and never un otro: otra escalera.

words.es: No hay nadie en el andamio.
words.note: Spanish keeps both negatives: no hay nadie.

words.en: We never work without safety glasses.
words.es: Nunca trabajamos sin lentes de seguridad.

lessons.speaking: Tell a coworker what is missing, what has not arrived yet, and what the crew needs more or less of today.

lessons.title: Polite Requests and Commands
lessons.objective: Ask a worker politely for help and give simple usted commands on site.
lessons.focus: ¿Puede…? for polite requests and usted commands like traiga, ponga, pare

words.en: Can you bring the ladder, please?

words.note: Usted command to one person; to the crew: pongan.
To the whole crew: Pónganse el casco.

words.en: Can you help me with the beam?
Stop work and call the supervisor.
words.es: Pare el trabajo y llame al supervisor.
words.note: Personal a before a person: llame al supervisor.

lessons.speaking: Ask a worker politely to bring a pallet and help you with a beam, then give two simple usted commands.

lessons.title: Words You Already Know and Getting Help
lessons.objective: Recognize jobsite cognates and use survival phrases when you do not understand.
lessons.focus: Cognates ending in -ción, -dad and -ente, plus survival phrases for getting help

words.note: -ción words are feminine and match English -tion.
-dad words are feminine and match English -ty.
For a woman: la clienta.

words.en: Can you speak more slowly, please?

words.note: Ustedes command to everyone nearby.

words.en: I need help with the installation.

lessons.speaking: Tell a coworker you speak a little Spanish, ask them to speak more slowly, and ask what a jobsite word means.
